Interest is payable semi-annually at 6.500% through May 15, 2037, then quarterly at CME Term SOFR (3-month) plus 2.120% plus a 0.26161% spread adjustment. The debentures are redeemable at par (plus accrued interest) on/after May 15, 2037, or earlier under certain circumstances at a make-whole price. The Company may defer interest for up to 10 consecutive years (with compounding), subject to a common stock issuance obligation (75 million shares reserved) if funds cannot otherwise be raised, and dividend/redemption restrictions apply during deferral. The debentures are also subject to a Replacement Capital Covenant benefiting holders of the $800 million Floating Rate Subordinated Debentures due 2053.

answer: Over 2023–2024, Zillow pursued small, software-focused "tuck-in" acquisitions (Aryeo, Spruce, Follow Up Boss in 2023; Virtual Staging AI in 2024) rather than large-scale M&A, spending ~$433 million in 2023 (mainly the $399M Follow Up Boss deal) versus only ~$7 million in 2024. These deals were explicitly designed to build an integrated software/transaction-management ecosystem for real estate professionals. answer: The Junior Subordinated Debentures are Series A 6.500% Fixed-to-Floating Rate securities with $500 million outstanding as of Dec 31, 2024. Scheduled maturity is May 15, 2057 (final maturity May 15, 2067). Interest is paid semi-annually at the fixed 6.500% rate until May 15, 2037, then quarterly at three-month SOFR (CME Term SOFR) plus 2.120% plus a 0.26161% spread adjustment. Redeemable in whole/part on/after May 15, 2037 at par plus accrued interest, or earlier under certain circumstances at par or make-whole price. The Company may defer interest for up to 10 consecutive years (compounding), during which common/preferred dividends are prohibited; 75 million shares of common stock are reserved to satisfy potential deferred-interest settlement obligations. The debentures are subject to a Replacement Capital Covenant (RCC) restricting early repayment/redemption absent replacement capital, benefiting holders of the $800 million Floating Rate Subordinated Debentures due 2053, terminating in 2067 (or earlier under specified conditions).

answer: At the consolidated level, virtually all (~100%) of Uber's 18% FY2024 revenue growth ($6.7B increase, from $37,281M to $43,978M) was driven by Gross Bookings/volume growth (also +18%, or +21% constant currency), not take-rate expansion — the implied consolidated take rate (revenue/Gross Bookings) was essentially flat at ~27.0% in both years (27.04% in 2023 vs. 27.02% in 2024). At the segment level, Mobility's take rate expanded modestly (revenue +26% vs. Gross Bookings +~21%) while Delivery's take rate compressed (revenue +13% vs. Gross Bookings +~17%, partly due to a $713M contra-revenue reclassification and offset by a $461M advertising revenue gain), and these effects roughly offset in the consolidated figures.

answer: Yes — Workday discloses a **Gross Revenue Retention Rate** (approximately 98% as of January 31, 2025). No separate "net" retention metric is disclosed in this filing.

answer: Over the trailing two years, Zillow's acquisition activity was concentrated entirely in calendar 2023 (Aryeo – $35M, 7/31/23; Spruce – $19M, 9/12/23; Follow Up Boss – $399M cash + up to $100M contingent consideration, 12/8/23; total ~$453M consideration, adding ~$444M of goodwill), all aimed at building an "integrated software experience" for the residential real-estate transaction (CRM, listing media, title/escrow). No new acquisitions were made in FY2024 (only a $7M immaterial true-up payment; goodwill essentially flat at $2,817M→$2,823M). This M&A reinforced the Residential/Mortgage ("Sales") revenue lines, which still made up ~78% of FY2024 revenue ($1,739M of $2,236M) though growing modestly (+6% vs 2022), while Rentals — the fastest-growing segment (+65% to $453M, now ~20% of revenue) — grew organically without acquisitions. answer: Over FY2023–FY2024, Zillow's M&A was concentrated in late calendar 2023 with three tuck-in deals — Aryeo (Aug 2023, $15M net cash), Spruce (Sep 2023, $19M net cash), and Follow Up Boss (Dec 2023, $399M net cash / $484M total consideration) — totaling ~$433M net cash paid for acquisitions in FY2023, all real-estate-agent-facing software businesses generating goodwill of $26M, $16M and $402M respectively. In FY2024, acquisition spend fell to just $7M net cash (goodwill rose only $6M, from $2,817M to $2,823M), indicating no new material acquisitions closed in 2024 — a pause after the 2023 deal-making. Meanwhile total revenue grew from $1,958M (FY2022) to $1,945M (FY2023, flat) to $2,236M (FY2024, +15%), with Residential revenue's share of the mix declining (77.7%→74.7%→71.3%) even though the FY2023 acquisitions targeted the Residential/agent ecosystem, while Rentals revenue (which received no acquisition investment) grew fastest in both dollars ($274M→$453M) and mix share (14.0%→20.3%). Mortgages revenue also recovered ($96M→$145M). This suggests the 2023 tuck-ins were aimed at strengthening the core Residential/agent-technology stack, while the actual revenue-mix shift toward Rentals and the FY2024 growth reacceleration were driven organically rather than by new acquisitions, consistent with a 2024 focus on integrating prior deals rather than new M&A.

answer: As of December 31, 2024, Allstate's Junior Subordinated Debentures consisted of $500 million outstanding of Series A 6.500% Fixed-to-Floating Rate Junior Subordinated Debentures, due 2067 (scheduled maturity May 15, 2057; final maturity May 15, 2067). Interest is 6.500% fixed, paid semi-annually, through May 15, 2037, then floats quarterly at three-month SOFR (formerly LIBOR) plus 2.120% plus a 0.26161% spread adjustment. Redeemable in whole/part at principal plus accrued interest on or after May 15, 2037 (or earlier in limited circumstances at principal plus accrued interest or a make-whole price). Allstate may defer interest for up to 10 consecutive years (compounding), during which it cannot pay common/preferred dividends or repurchase stock, and has reserved 75 million common shares to help fund deferred interest if needed. The debentures are subject to a Replacement Capital Covenant restricting early repayment/redemption absent qualifying equity-like proceeds, benefiting holders of designated "covered debt" (currently the $800 million Floating Rate Subordinated Debentures due 2053) rather than the Junior Subordinated Debenture holders themselves; the RCC terminates in 2067.

answer: Yes — Workday discloses a **Gross Revenue Retention Rate** (approximately 98% as of January 31, 2025) in the MD&A section of its FY2025 10-K. It is defined as the percentage of recurring revenue (based on Annualized Recurring Revenue, "ARR") retained from the same set of existing customers year-over-year: prior-period-end ARR for a customer cohort compared to that same cohort's ARR at the current period-end. It captures revenue lost to churn but excludes any revenue gained from upsells/expansions (add-ons, volume or price increases). No separate "net revenue retention rate" metric is disclosed in this filing.

These deals target the residential transaction workflow (agent tools, listings, closing services) rather than adding new revenue categories, and management called them immaterial to consolidated pro-forma results. Meanwhile, revenue mix shifted organically: Residential fell from ~78% of revenue (2022) to 71% (2024, $1,594M) even as it grew modestly; Rentals surged 65% over the same period ($274M→$453M, now 20% of revenue) and Mortgages rose 22% ($119M→$145M, +51% in 2024 alone) — both driven by internal investment (Rentals marketplace/multifamily partnerships, Zillow Home Loans expansion), not M&A. So the acquisition strategy reinforced the still-dominant Residential/For-Sale transaction funnel via software integration, while the real revenue-mix diversification toward Rentals and Mortgages came from organic investment rather than acquisitions.

This acquisition focus reinforces the Residential/Mortgages ("For Sale") side of the business even as the actual revenue mix has been shifting away from it — For Sale revenue fell from ~84% of total revenue in FY2022 to ~78% in FY2024, while Rentals revenue (grown organically, not via acquisition) rose from 14.0% to 20.3% of total revenue ($274M→$453M). So the acquisition strategy supports/consolidates the core Residential transaction business rather than chasing the segment (Rentals) that is actually gaining share of the revenue mix.

answer: Zillow's M&A was concentrated almost entirely in 2023, not 2024. In 2023 it closed three tuck‑in, technology‑enabling acquisitions — Aryeo ($35M, photography software), Spruce ($19M cash, title/escrow tech) and Follow Up Boss ($484M total consideration: $403M cash + up to $100M contingent consideration, real‑estate agent CRM/software) — spending about $433 million net cash on acquisitions that year. In FY2024, Zillow made essentially no new acquisitions (only ~$7 million of acquisition-related cash outflow, versus $433 million in 2023; goodwill rose only $6 million to $2,823 million), indicating a shift to integrating the 2023 purchases rather than new dealmaking. This pattern aligns with the evolving revenue mix: while core Residential (for-sale/Premier Agent) revenue grew only modestly (+4.7% from FY2022's $1,522M to FY2024's $1,594M) and remains ~71% of total revenue, Rentals revenue jumped 65% ($274M→$453M) and Mortgages grew 22% ($119M→$145M, +51% in 2024 alone) over the same two years, out of total revenue growth from $1,958M (2022) to $2,236M (2024). The 2023 acquisitions were software/workflow tools embedded in the transaction funnel (CRM, listing media, closing/title tech) rather than stand-alone revenue segments, consistent with a "more integrated software experience" strategy that appears to have supported outsized growth in Rentals and Mortgages relative to legacy Residential advertising revenue by FY2024.

answer: Over the trailing two years, Zillow's M&A was concentrated entirely in H2 2023 — three tuck-in software/services acquisitions (Aryeo, ~$35M; Spruce, ~$19M; Follow Up Boss, ~$399M cash plus up to $100M contingent consideration) all aimed at real-estate-agent-facing tools (CRM, media production, title/escrow) to deepen Zillow's "housing super app"/integrated-transaction strategy — with essentially no new acquisitions in FY2024 (only ~$7M in acquisition-related cash outflow, per us-gaap:PaymentsToAcquireBusinessesNetOfCashAcquired). These deals reinforced the Residential (agent) revenue line, whose dollar revenue grew ($1,522M→$1,594M FY22–FY24) but whose share of total revenue actually fell (~78%→~71%), while Rentals — not a target of acquisition spend — grew fastest organically, rising from 14% to over 20% of total revenue ($274M→$453M). So the acquisition strategy strengthened the core agent/transaction ecosystem via software capability rather than chasing the segment (Rentals) that is actually driving the shift in revenue mix, and FY2024 shows a pause in dealmaking in favor of integrating the 2023 purchases.
